name: Producer-Consumer and Bounded Queues
intent: Decouple the code that creates work from the code that does it with a queue, and decide how big the queue may get and what happens when it is full, so that a fast producer cannot bury a slow consumer.
scenario: One producer offers 2 items per tick for 60 ticks, 120 items in all, to 3 consumers that each need 2 ticks per item, so together they take only 1.5 items per tick. We try an unbounded queue and a queue bounded to 10 or to 1, with three ways to handle a full queue (block the producer, drop the newest item, drop the oldest), and consumers that put failed items back on the same queue.
problem: A producer and a consumer rarely run at the same speed. A queue between them absorbs short bursts, which is its job. But when the producer is faster for long enough, the queue only moves the problem: an unbounded queue grows until memory runs out, and every item waits longer than the last. Something has to say no, and the question is who, when, and at what cost.

howItWorks.title: A queue decouples the two sides
howItWorks.text: The producer puts items in, the consumers take them out, and neither waits for the other while the queue has room and items. That smooths bursts: if the producer pauses, the consumers keep working; if the consumers stall for a moment, the producer does not notice. The queue holds the difference between the two rates.

howItWorks.title: Sustained overload cannot be absorbed
howItWorks.text: If items arrive faster than they are taken, for long enough, the queue keeps growing. In the model, 2 items per tick against a capacity of 1.5 grows the unbounded queue to 31 items and makes the longest wait 21 ticks. Nothing fails, so nothing alerts you, until memory or latency does.

howItWorks.title: A bound makes overload visible
howItWorks.text: Bounding the queue (here, to 10) puts a ceiling on memory and on how long an accepted item waits in the queue: 7 ticks instead of 21. The model counts only time inside the queue; when the producer is blocked, the rest of the delay has not gone away, it now waits upstream, before the item is accepted. The cost is that something must happen when the queue is full. Pick that deliberately: block the producer, drop the newest item, or drop the oldest.

howItWorks.title: Block, or drop: who bears the cost
howItWorks.text: Blocking the producer passes the slowdown upstream (backpressure): nothing is lost, the producer is held up for 28 ticks, and the run ends no later than the unbounded one. Dropping loses work: 21 items here. Dropping the newest keeps old items (good when order matters and the producer can retry); dropping the oldest keeps the freshest (good for live readings, where the latest value is the one that counts).

howItWorks.title: Size the bound and watch the high-water mark
howItWorks.text: A bound too small starves the consumers: with a limit of 1 they take only 1 item per tick and the run takes 123 ticks instead of 83. Too large and it hides overload and wastes memory. Track the high-water mark (the most items ever queued) and how often the producer is blocked or items dropped: they tell you whether the bound is right. And never let a consumer put work back on the queue it is draining while the queue can block: it can deadlock.

pros: Producer and consumer run at their own pace, and bursts are smoothed out
A bounded queue caps memory and the maximum wait of an accepted item
Blocking the producer applies backpressure: the slowdown reaches whoever causes the load
The high-water mark and the drop count show overload long before it becomes an outage
cons: A queue only hides a rate mismatch, it cannot fix one: sustained overload needs more consumers or less input
An unbounded queue turns overload into silent memory growth and ever-longer waits
Blocking can stall the producer, and anything waiting on it, for as long as the consumers are slow
Dropping loses work, so it is only right when the work can be lost or redone
whenToUse: Work that arrives in bursts and can be processed a little later, such as emails, thumbnails and log lines
Stages of a pipeline that run at different speeds
Protecting a slow downstream (a database, a third-party API) from a fast upstream
whenNotToUse: Requests where the caller needs the answer now and a long wait is worth nothing: reject early instead
Work that cannot be lost or reordered, with a drop policy
Consumers that re-queue their own failures onto a bounded, blocking queue
pitfalls: An unbounded queue: with sustained overload it grows without limit, and the model's longest wait (21 ticks) keeps rising with the run length
A bound of 1 or 2 'to be safe': it forces the producer and consumers to move in lockstep and starves the consumers
Choosing drop-newest or drop-oldest without asking which items matter: they lose different items (item 37 against item 27 in the model)
A consumer that puts a failed item back on the same bounded, blocking queue: when every consumer does it at once, none can take anything and the pipeline deadlocks at tick 28
Blocking the producer inside a thread that also serves other work, so the stall spreads
Not measuring: without the high-water mark and the drop and blocked counts, you cannot tell a healthy queue from one about to fail

roles.label: Producer
roles.description: Creates items of work at its own rate.

roles.label: Queue
roles.description: Holds items between the producer and the consumers.

roles.label: Consumers
roles.description: Take items out and process them, 2 ticks each.

roles.label: Upstream callers
roles.description: Whoever feeds the producer, and feels any slowdown.

quiz.question: A producer offers 2 items per tick to consumers that can take 1.5 per tick, through an unbounded queue. What happens as the run goes on?
options: The queue settles at a fixed size, because consumers speed up when it is long.
The queue shrinks, because a queue can only hold what the consumers can process.
The queue keeps growing, so memory use and the wait for each new item keep rising.
The queue drops items on its own once it is longer than the producer's burst.
quiz.explanation: Items arrive faster than they leave, and an unbounded queue never pushes back, so the backlog grows by half an item every tick. Memory and waiting time rise with it, and nothing fails until a resource runs out.

quiz.question: A service buffers live temperature readings for a display, and the queue is full. Which policy suits it best?
options: Block the producer, so every reading is kept and shown in the order it was taken.
Drop the newest reading, so the oldest reading in the queue is always shown first.
Grow the queue without limit, so that no reading is ever lost.
Drop the oldest reading, because only the most recent values are of use to the display.
quiz.explanation: For live values the latest reading is the one that matters, and a stale one has no value. Dropping the oldest keeps the queue fresh. Blocking or dropping the newest would show old data, and an unbounded queue would show it later and later.

quiz.question: Consumers put failed items back on the same bounded queue, and the producer blocks when it is full. Under load the whole pipeline stops. Why?
options: Retried items are always processed first, so new items starve until the queue is empty.
When the queue is full, every consumer is waiting to put an item back, so none takes one out.
A failed item makes the queue lock itself until an operator clears it.
The producer blocks on failed items, and a blocked producer cannot be woken up again.
quiz.explanation: Only consumers can make room, and they are all stuck waiting for room: a cycle, so a deadlock. Use a separate retry queue, a non-blocking put, or a dead-letter queue instead of feeding the queue you are draining.
